stances.claim: At the request of CJ Gesmundo, CJP represented the Philippines in the recent ASEAN Law Association (ALA) 'Inaugural Lecture Series on Gender Justice' in Kuala Lumpur, sponsored by the Malaysian Supreme Court and keynoted by ALA President and former Malaysian CJ Tun Tengku Maimun binti Tuan Mat -- whose lecture was both 'intellectually rigorous and deeply humane,' grounded in constitutional interpretation yet attentive to lived realities in societies shaped by multiple legal traditions.

Many ASEAN countries, including Malaysia and the Philippines, uphold legal pluralism -- the coexistence of multiple laws within one nation. The Philippine legal system blends civil and common law, though it also recognizes the customary laws of indigenous peoples under the IPRA and the Code of Muslim Personal Law (PD 1083).

Notably, President Marcos approved in 2024 the creation of three new Shari'a Judicial Districts and 12 additional Shari'a Circuit Courts -- these courts, as first codified by his late father, enforce PD 1083 adjudicating marriage, divorce, and inheritance, areas where gender-equality issues are relevant.

Bondagjy v. Bondagjy (Dec 7 2001) correctly ruled that a custody proceeding between two Muslim parents should be decided according to ordinary Philippine civil law if one parent -- whose fitness to care for the child became the issue -- has converted to a non-Muslim faith; the SC held that the best interest of the child should have the highest priority and affirmed the maternal preference in the custody of young children.

CJ Maimun rightly articulated that the challenge is not to deny pluralism but to ensure that constitutional guarantees of equality prevail when plural systems collide with fundamental rights -- 'Equality does not always demand identical treatment in all circumstances. What it requires is that any difference in treatment must rest on an intelligible differentia and that such differentia must bear a rational nexus to the objective of the law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Maimun verbatim citation + intelligible-differentia + rational-nexus equality-test

stances.claim: The Philippines can be proud of its track record in advancing gender justice and overcoming challenges posed by both legal and religious pluralism -- as a predominantly Catholic country, religious teachings (particularly biblical views on women and life) continue to influence social attitudes and at times policy debates. Husbands citing the Bible insist that wives must be submissive to their husbands as to the Lord -- they however forget the crucial portion that follows: husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the Church to the point of death.

The Constitution is clear in recognizing the role of women in nation-building and ensuring the fundamental equality of women and men before the law -- over the years these constitutional commitments have been translated into laws and influenced legal decisions.

While still an Associate Justice, CJP penned People v. Genosa (Jan 15 2004) -- adopting for the first time the 'battered woman syndrome' as a form of self-defense, or at least as a mitigating circumstance, in a prosecution for parricide committed by a wife against her husband; the ruling acknowledged the mental state of a pregnant woman who at the time of the crime had endured sustained and medically documented abuse by her spouse for over 13 years.

The Philippines was the first ASEAN country to ratify Cedaw in 1981 and locally adopted the convention's measures through the Magna Carta for Women (RA 9710) -- in CJ Maimun's words, 'Cedaw serves as a bridge in harmonizing diverse legal traditions with universal principles of equality, justice, and fairness.' The Malaysian highest court committed to Cedaw in ruling that pregnancy cannot be a legal basis for gender discrimination.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-ASEAN-ratifier + Maimun verbatim Cedaw-as-bridge + Malaysian-pregnancy-discrimination ruling-citation

stances.claim: The SC reiterated its transformative work in fulfilling 'Equal and Inclusive Justice' via its Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations (SPJI 2022-2027) -- specifically in the '2025 Campaign to End Violence Against Women,' the Court stressed that 'vigilance, clarity, and empathy must be continuing standards in decision-making.'

As CJ Maimun concluded, gender justice transcends legal systems and borders -- legal pluralism is not a barrier but a source of strength; it should not become an excuse to perpetuate inequality but rather a pathway toward a more inclusive and just regional order. CJP humbly adds that gender justice is not about privileging women over men, but about fairness, dignity, and assuring that our legal systems -- plural as they may be -- do not leave more than half of our population marginalized and vulnerable.
stances.confidence: asserted as closing redefinition of gender justice

one_paragraph_summary: At Chief Justice Gesmundo's request, Panganiban represented the Philippines at the ASEAN Law Association's Inaugural Lecture Series on Gender Justice in Kuala Lumpur, keynoted by former Malaysian Chief Justice Tun Tengku Maimun. He surveys Philippine legal pluralism -- civil law, common law, IPRA-recognized indigenous customary law, and PD 1083's Code of Muslim Personal Law (expanded by Marcos's 2024 creation of three new Shari'a Judicial Districts and 12 Circuit Courts) -- and shows how constitutional equality should prevail when plural systems collide with fundamental rights. He cites Bondagjy on inter-religious custody, his own authorship of People v. Genosa (2004) adopting battered woman syndrome, the Philippines' first-in-ASEAN 1981 Cedaw ratification, and the Magna Carta for Women, alongside the Malaysian ruling that pregnancy cannot ground gender discrimination. Endorsing CJ Maimun's intelligible-differentia framework, he reframes gender justice as fairness and dignity ensuring no plural system leaves more than half the population marginalized.
